article_title: Access to Powerful Technology as a Catalyst for Career Pathway Engagement
citation: Wortman, A., and Schiner, N. (2024, June). Access to powerful technology as a catalyst for career pathway engagement [Project Report]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/217
title: HP Learning Studio at Anaheim High School
description: The HP Learning Studio is a school-community technology space launched in Winter 2024 at Anaheim High School, featuring "high-end HP workstations running Windows 11 and powered by the latest Intel processors, scholastic esports peripherals, and prosumer-grade audio-visual and broadcasting equipment." It is deliberately not tied to any one teacher's class or club, sits in the center of campus, and provides access to broadcasting, graphic design, podcasting, computer science, audiovisual, and esports equipment so students not enrolled in CTE pathways can explore interests. Equipment selection prioritized versatility, power, and long-term value, with modular PCs that can be upgraded.
requirements: A needs assessment and educator leadership team to inform space and equipment selection; school-community-industry partnerships to support CTE awareness, interest, and engagement
constraints: CTE facilities at the school were previously accessible only to enrolled pathway students; the studio addresses but does not eliminate broader access limitations
target_learners: high school students, including historically and systemically excluded youth not enrolled in CTE pathways
target_learning_goals: exploration of career interests, CTE pathway awareness and engagement, authentic project-based learning
examples: Launch stations included physics simulations, esports play, a HyperX ProCast podcasting station, and EV3 Mindstorms robot coding demonstrations
key_sources: Wortman, A., and Schiner, N. (2024, June). Access to powerful technology as a catalyst for career pathway engagement [Project Report]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/217

article_title: The handwriting programming language for primary school: aligning computer science education with established teaching practices
citation: Brender, J., El-Hamamsy, L., Giang, C., Mathex, L., Käser, T., & Mondada, F. (2025). The handwriting programming language for primary school: aligning computer science education with established teaching practices. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10503-z
title: The handwriting programming language (HPL) system
description: The HPL system is a computer-vision-based interface that lets students write handwritten program instructions on paper, take a picture with a web-app, and send the decoded commands to a virtual or physical agent (the Thymio robot) for execution. It uses the Google Cloud Vision API to convert handwriting into strings, then maps them to commands via Levenshtein edit distance, with a set of 17 pre-defined instructions that can be expanded. It was designed following the educational robotics learning systems (ERLS) framework and constructive alignment principles, with special attention to aligning with existing primary school classroom practices.
requirements: Requires a device with a camera and web access to run the web-based application
Requires the Google Cloud Vision API for handwriting character recognition
Requires an agent (virtual or physical) to execute the decoded commands
constraints: Implemented for use with the Thymio robot and a syntax resembling Scratch
The mapping was implemented in French and in English but can be adapted to any language decodable by Google Cloud Vision's API
target_learning_goals: Computer science concepts including sequences, loops, and conditional statements
examples: Students write their solution, one line per instruction, in a box in the activity book, then photograph it with the web-app
key_sources: Brender, J., El-Hamamsy, L., Giang, C., Mathex, L., Käser, T., & Mondada, F. (2025). The handwriting programming language for primary school: aligning computer science education with established teaching practices. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10503-z

article_title: Food for thought? The effects of the Healthy Primary School of the Future on children's educational outcomes.
citation: van Engelen Bo H. W., Hahnraths Marla T. H., Winkens Bjorn, Schils Trudie, van Schayck Onno C. P. (2026). Food for thought? The effects of the Healthy Primary School of the Future on children's educational outcomes. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0334638
title: Healthy Primary School of the Future (HPSF) intervention
description: HPSF is a Dutch school-based health intervention developed by the schoolboard, regional public health services, and Maastricht University aiming to "sustainably integrate health in the school system". It consisted of two main changes: "1) daily provision of a free healthy school lunch, and 2) daily structured 60-minute PA sessions after lunch." The school day was extended to prolong the lunch break by 45-75 minutes; lunches were designed by a dietician, varied every ten weeks, and at least 80% of products met Dutch Health Council dietary guidelines. Full schools implemented both components; partial schools implemented physical activity only.
requirements: Structured physical activity sessions guided by teachers, pedagogical staff, and/or members of local sports clubs
Extended school day providing 45-75 minutes of additional lunch break time
constraints: The study did not include a group receiving only the healthy school lunch, so the lunch component's isolated effect could not be reported
target_learners: Primary school children aged 6-12 years (study years 3-8)
examples: Two full HPSF schools provided daily healthy lunches and structured PA sessions; two partial HPSF schools provided PA sessions only; four control schools continued their regular curriculum
key_sources: van Engelen Bo H. W., Hahnraths Marla T. H., Winkens Bjorn, Schils Trudie, van Schayck Onno C. P. (2026). Food for thought? The effects of the Healthy Primary School of the Future on children's educational outcomes. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0334638

article_title: Primary Mental Health Competencies for Hospice and Palliative Medicine Physicians: A Delphi Study.
citation: Podgurski L, Chammas D, Brenner KO, Rosenberg LB, Goyal NG, Lapid MI, Morris SE, Pirl WF, Sumser B, Thompson BW, Wright L, Shalev D. (2025). Primary Mental Health Competencies for Hospice and Palliative Medicine Physicians: A Delphi Study. Journal of Pain and Symptom Management. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpainsymman.2025.05.009
title: Final consensus competency framework in three categories (Tables 2–4)
description: The final competency framework comprises 32 consensus competencies across three categories: psychological foundations of serious illness care (Table 2), psychiatric disorders in serious illness (Table 3), and systems-based practice (Table 4). Tables list specific competencies such as recognizing "normative emotional reactions to serious illness", diagnosing and providing first-line management for conditions including major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, adjustment disorders, delirium, and opioid use disorder, and navigating mental health resources within and outside the interdisciplinary team. Psychological concepts are listed as key terms to direct further learning.
requirements: Intended for specialist HPM physicians; competencies assume interdisciplinary team collaboration
constraints: Competency definition is described as just the first step, with curriculum development, implementation, and evaluation still needed
target_learning_goals: Primary mental health knowledge and skills in palliative care
key_sources: Podgurski L, Chammas D, Brenner KO, Rosenberg LB, Goyal NG, Lapid MI, Morris SE, Pirl WF, Sumser B, Thompson BW, Wright L, Shalev D. (2025). Primary Mental Health Competencies for Hospice and Palliative Medicine Physicians: A Delphi Study. Journal of Pain and Symptom Management. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpainsymman.2025.05.009

article_title: Expanding worldviews on psychometric analysis of measurement tools in health professions education and research.
citation: Lazarus Michelle D., Sarkar Mahbub, Palermo Claire, Soh Sze‐Ee, Farlie Melanie K. (2025). Expanding worldviews on psychometric analysis of measurement tools in health professions education and research. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70053
title: Research worldviews in HPE: ontology, epistemology, methodology, axiology, and four prominent worldviews with historically associated methods
description: The article defines worldviews through Varpio et al.'s dimensions: ontology (nature of reality), epistemology (what can be known), methodology (how knowledge is accessed), and axiology (research values). It then organizes four prominent worldviews—"positivism/post‐positivism, interpretivism, critical inquiry, and pragmatism"—each with key assumptions and historically associated methodological approaches (quantitative designs and psychometrics for positivism; case studies, ethnography, interviews for interpretivism; mixed-methods typologies for pragmatism; co-production and decolonising methodologies for critical approaches), illustrated in Table 1 and Figure 1.
requirements: Researchers need to state their assumptions about reality, knowledge, methods, and values, since ontological and epistemological assumptions shape methodology choice
constraints: The article notes that contemporarily the relationship between methods and worldviews remains unclear, with historically rigid worldview–method alignments now having fuzzy borders
target_learners: health professions education researchers and educators
target_learning_goals: understanding how worldviews shape research design, measurement practices, and interpretation in HPE
examples: Table 1 pairs each worldview with example research questions, such as positivist anxiety measurement versus interpretivist study of students' emotional experience of donor dissection
key_sources: Lazarus Michelle D., Sarkar Mahbub, Palermo Claire, Soh Sze‐Ee, Farlie Melanie K. (2025). Expanding worldviews on psychometric analysis of measurement tools in health professions education and research. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70053
